title: APT16
summary: APT16 is a cluster name for espionage activity that public reporting links to China-nexus operators and describes as small-scale and targeted, with an emphasis on media organisations, journalists, and government bodies in East Asia. Reporting associates it with a small set of campaigns that combined spearphishing messages containing malicious links and documents with server-side exploitation of internet-facing services, and it has been described in relation to a larger campaign publicly attributed to a related group, which is one reason the boundary between the two labels is unclear. Public documentation is limited and in places single-source, so statements about capability should stay cautious. Defenders detect the activity through mail records showing credential harvesting links, web server logs showing exploitation attempts against public services, and endpoint evidence of document readers spawning script interpreters. The common misunderstanding is that a low-profile, lightly documented group is therefore a low threat. Limited reporting reflects limited observation, not limited capability, and the targeting of journalists carries consequences that reach beyond one organisation.

beginner.definition: APT16 is a research name for a small cyber spying group that public reports link to China. It has targeted news organisations, journalists, and government offices in East Asia. It uses fake login pages and harmful documents to steal access.
beginner.whyItMatters: Journalists and newsrooms hold sources and private conversations. When those are stolen, real people can be put at risk, not just the company. This group is documented less than others, so you must assume gaps in what is known. Targets include public-facing websites that anyone can reach. That means your internet-facing services need attention, not only your internal network.
howItWorks: The attackers gather the names and email addresses of journalists and government officials.
They send emails holding a link to a fake login page, and it copies whatever is typed.
The page copies the real one and captures whatever the reader types.
Other emails carry documents that run code when the reader allows it.
They also scan public websites for flaws that would let them break in without a password.
Once inside, they read mail, follow conversations, and copy the documents that matter.
beginner.example: Imagine a reception desk that takes messages for every journalist in a busy newsroom. A caller claims to be a source. He asks the receptionist to confirm a password so the message can be delivered. The receptionist is helpful and confirms it. Nothing was broken and no lock was picked. The information simply walked out through a normal conversation. Fake login pages and credential phishing follow this pattern. The attacker never attacks the system. The attacker asks a helpful person for the key, and the person hands it over.
takeaways: Fake login pages steal passwords without touching your systems.
Journalists and their sources face risk when accounts are taken over.
Public websites need the same care as internal servers.

objectives: Explain how credential harvesting pages capture credentials without exploiting software.
Describe how internet-facing service exploitation complements phishing in a campaign.
Identify web server and mail log evidence of this activity pattern.
Explain why limited public reporting does not imply limited capability.
Describe the harm to sources and individuals when media accounts are compromised.
Explain why cluster boundaries between related groups can be genuinely unclear.
